tip: Many adjectives add ‘-are’ to make comparatives: ‘billig’ becomes ‘billigare’, cheaper.
‘Sin’ points back to the subject and means one's own: ‘sin väska’ is her own bag, not someone else's.
Swedish often uses ‘ligger’ for things resting flat: ‘böckerna ligger på bordet’, the books are on the table.
‘Allemansrätten’ allows everyone to walk, camp, and pick berries on almost any land.
‘Om’ means if or whether in an indirect question: ‘hon frågade om vi hade ätit’.
In the definite plural the adjective normally ends in ‘-a’ and the noun in ‘-na’: ‘de smala gatorna’.
‘Än’ after a question word means no matter: ‘hur du än gör’, no matter what you do.
The definite article is normally a suffix, not a separate word: ‘golv’ plus ‘-et’ gives ‘golvet’, the floor.
Some ‘-el’ nouns shorten before the definite ending: ‘himmel’ becomes ‘himlen’, not ‘himmelen’ (the ‘e’ and one ‘m’ drop).
‘Som’ means who, which or that for all genders and numbers, as in ‘pojken som springer’.
‘Var’ is the past tense of ‘vara’ (to be); the present is ‘är’, as in ‘dagen var lång’.
Many adverbs are just the adjective plus ‘-t’: ‘snabb’ (quick) becomes ‘snabbt’ (quickly).
Swedish glues nouns into compounds: ‘jul’ (Christmas) plus ‘bord’ (table) makes ‘julbord’.
‘Kläder’ (clothes) exists only in the plural; the definite form ‘kläderna’ has no singular counterpart.
With an adjective, the definite is marked twice, on the article and the noun ending, and the adjective takes ‘-a’: ‘den starka vinden’.
‘Hem’ means toward home (movement), ‘hemma’ means at home (location); ‘vägen hem’ is the way homeward.
‘Gå igenom’ is a two-part verb meaning to review or go through; in speech the stress falls on ‘igenom’.
‘Kom’ is the irregular past of ‘komma’ (to come); the present is ‘kommer’, as in ‘jag kom från ett möte’.
Many ‘ett’-words are identical in singular and plural: ‘ett träd’, ‘flera träd’; the definite plural adds ‘-en’, ‘träden’.
Many ‘en’-words take ‘-ar’ in the plural, then add ‘-na’ for the definite: ‘en stol’, ‘stolar’, ‘stolarna’.
The ‘-s’ ending can mean doing something to each other: ‘följas åt’ is to accompany each other, as in ‘de följs åt’.
‘Hon’ (she) becomes ‘henne’ as an object: ‘jag ringer henne’ means I call her.
Seasons normally use ‘på’ plus the definite form: ‘på sommaren’ = in summer, ‘på vintern’ = in winter.
‘Få blod på tand’ literally means to get blood on the tooth; it means to get eager for more.
Add ‘som helst’ to a question word for any at all: ‘vem som helst’ = anyone, ‘vad som helst’ = anything.
‘Kommer att’ plus a verb expresses the future, often for predictions: ‘det kommer snart att vara vår’ (‘snart’ slips in between).
‘Fika’ works as both noun and verb for a coffee-and-cake break: ‘ta en fika’ = have a coffee break.
After ‘samma’ the noun stays in its base form, no definite ending: ‘samma båt’, not ‘samma båten’.
‘Det var ... som’ highlights one part of the sentence: ‘det var hon som hade rätt’ puts the focus on ‘hon’.
Swedish often uses a position verb where English says is: ‘står’ (stands) for upright things, so ‘stolen står i hörnet’.
